raw_comment:
The article does not look at all the consequences of increasing elderly populations in the West. Food Production in the US will dramatically start to decrease within the next few decades, due to labor shortages. Relying wholly on mechanization or immigrant labor will not be sufficient and we will not be able to meet the food demands of the developing world. The population growth rates of some in the developing world, are linked to access to Western grain and corn imports. If and when these decrease, there will be massive famine in Africa. It's attenuated and counter-intuitive, but it will happen.

Africa will have a huge population of younger working-age population. But they will not be able to reap any of the benefits of this, because food imports, medical aid imports, all these things that Africa needs from more advanced nations will be pulled back and decreased, as these older nations go into a cocoon-like state of demographic hibernation. Africa may suffer greatly when this happens. Or, perhaps, they will immigrate to a de-populated Europe and America and find sparsely populated vacant cities, farming fields, and abandoned industrial plants---all just waiting for people to man the levers of production.

I notice that as the graph progresses to the right with more cumulative force, the higher the percentages/changes of acquiring CTE become. I also notice that the chances of the further stages increase the more cumulative force is exerted.

 What do you wonder?
I wonder what precautions could be taken to prevent such diseases from occurring.  Have scientists tried using the composition of a woodpecker's head and brain to try and create some sort of design to aid in the invention of a specialized helmet?

How does this relate to me and my community?
Sports organizations may under pressure to adopt more stringent concussion policies, better helmet technology, and improved coaching methods to reduce brain injuries. A safer atmosphere for athletes may result from this. The local economy may be impacted if CTE worries cause a drop in participation or viewership in local sports programs. Businesses that depend on sporting events, such sports equipment shops and eateries close to stadiums, could be harmed.

As a Professional Data Consultant in 1995, I first bumped into the Baby Boom in a particual school district's data. I found that the early Boomers (1947-1956) became teachers in masses around 1966 as they entered collage. In 1995, after the typical 30 year carrer they began retireing in masses. This effect is occuring again now, with the second wave of generation X teachers.  
Now I am retired and writting a book, titled Echo, the effects of the Baby Boom.  And its not pretty.  I believe population data in the US is flawed.  I believe we are about to experience somthing like never before, where the replacement rate is so low, and the older boomers are about to die in an upward spike (as they were born) causing massive upheavals.  In 1995, I went down this rabbit hole of what if's.  Image a day, soon, where a business has requires 100 workers, and on that day 4 retire, and only one is available to hire. And the next day, 8 retire, and only one is again, availble to hire. By the third day, the business must shut down.  Schools in the Northeast USA are shutting down for lack of teachers AND students. Because the birth rate dropped since 1975, the US population is simply getting older. At 40%, its pure chaos 
We MAY be able to predict effects based on other old age population countries, but the information may be too late.
AI may solve the problem, but unitl the problem manifest itself, business may be reluctant in invest.  

I would love to communicate with regarding this topic.

Brazil also stays relatively stable and unchanging but in every graph shown. If the United States stays the same or relative population it is now, I don’t see much of an adjustment for us to be made. A good headline would probably be “Age Distributions Fluctuations Around The Globe? I Think Not!” This indicates the similarities between all three graphs, as they do not all change very much compared to each other.

2. raw_comment:
I notice that African countries have a constant trend of the majority young population. Similarly, South Asian countries such as Pakistan and India won’t reach a majority of older people by 2050 and instead have a majority of working-age individuals.  North and South American countries also don’t have a majority older population, but most European countries gradually go from a working-age population in 1990 to an older population in 2050.   

I wonder what factors impact this change; why do countries with high populations, such as India, continue having such a high population, but the age diversity doesn’t change? What variables haven’t the 2050 graph taken into account? How much will economies change based on the age distribution? How will federal systems to support senior citizens change in countries that will reach a majority older population?  Why do European countries experience such a drastic change in age distribution? How long will it take countries that haven’t reached an older population by 2050 to reach it?

This graph reflects the current lifespan averages of these countries, which is important to our community to understand better improvements that need to be made. Additionally, it allows us to prepare according to the anticipated economic changes. It also offers a prediction of what facilities will need to be made available according to the age demographic. 

I would name the graph Ages of Time.

1. What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?
The population bubbles grow as the years progress, meaning the population as a whole will grow. Africa seems
to be having a baby boom with lots of younger generational populations. India seems to be the biggest dot on
the graph, marking the most densely populated area.
2. What do you wonder?
What did the data look like in 1970, 1950, 1920?
DId Covid change the population at all?
Why is Africa's population growing so quickly?

Population growth affects the whole globe, but it also affects our generation as population growth leads to
a larger world hunger and a larger homeless population. With fewer resources to feed the growing
population, more people will suffer worse conditions. Furthermore, to make up for this lack of space,
more housing will be implemented further destroying natural areas and reservoirs that should be reserved.
Population growth is an imminent problem in our future that needs to be faced and helped. While we can't
stop population growth we can adapt our ways like creating more economical ways to farm and produce
other foods.

Population Growth in the World - How will we cope?

- Each panel is a **world map** with circles placed geographically.
- No stacking is used.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year (1990, 2023, 2050) | Temporal | **Faceting / panel title** |
| Geographic location (country position) | Categorical/nominal (geographic) | **Position on map** |
| Population magnitude (or country total represented by bubble size) | Quantitative | **Circle area/size** |
| Age structure / population age composition (younger → working age → older) | Ordinal | **Color/hue** of circles |
| Country name | Categorical/nominal | **Text label** |

- The color legend indicates an **ordered age-composition scale** from **younger populations** to **working age** to **older populations**.

raw_comment:
When comparing the 2023 age distribution chart to the 2050 one, I noticed that there is barely any variation/difference in age distribution in Africa. Africa seems to continue to have younger populations, which may be a result of high fertility/mortality rates. Is the average life expectancy low in Africa and how does that affect the labor force in Africa? Does Africa have to rely on its younger populations to make up the majority of its labor force? 
For the 2023 age distribution, I wonder if Japan prioritizes the health and well-being of its citizens more than other countries, which is leading it to have older populations. I also wonder if the Japanese government provides healthcare benefits/services to all of its citizens regardless of their economic situation. How does the Japanese government try to maintain a labor balance when it has a larger older population? Are there employment incentives to keep Japanese citizens from retiring early?

1. I noticed that most of the populations have become younger since 1990 but are going to be older in 2050.

2. I wonder what is causing there to be less younger populations in the future. Maybe this is because the average life expectancy could be increasing due to new medical advancements. I also wonder if this increase in aging populations would affect the economy in a negative way, since aging populations put pressure on society because the number of workers declines relative to the number of consumers.

3. This relates to my community because what will happen when the majority of people in the community are at retirement age and there are more consumers than people of working age.

This idea contrasts how we think kids are the key to the future although the population is mostly old.

raw_comment:
1) I notice that especially in Africa, as its populations in 1990 were few at the time, and younger it has a great increase throughout the years and continues to increase in younger populations as estimated for 2050. Only a few locations in the continent demonstrate populations of working age. Compared to the other continents it can be seen that generally places where there were younger populations in 1990, like the Americas as well as Asia, as the years passed to 2023 became working age, and so on to 2050 as the populations grew older. While in Europe, a lot of the population at working age in 1990, estimated to 2050 grow to be generally older populations. 

2) I wonder for locations where there is a surge in the younger population but a lack of older and working populations, will there be too many children but not enough adults? For the opposite, where there are large expected older populations, will there be issues in finding younger populations to care for them? 

3) As communities will each have to comply with their needs, some will probably need more schools for children, and other communities, nursing homes for the elders, this may require help from international nations to help cover these finances. By also having growing communities this could also cause trouble in all aspects from finding a job to a place to live. 

4) Many elders and babies to come, but will there be enough of us to tend to all?

- I'm curious how much medical systems play into the increasing population age; with a rise in the older population, so will overall healthcare costs. Furthermore, the inclusion of politics in the brief context also makes me wonder what role politics plays in the increasing older population and how it will impact the population moving forward.

- This relates to me and my community as increases in the older population will make finding jobs harder as the experience required may rise as well. Furthermore, the working population will also decrease the older the population gets. Lastly, my community already has a shortage of teachers, so a decrease in the overall working population by 2050 is concerning.

- Will Time Take Us? The Next Generation Nowhere To Be Seen

## 1) Chart type
- **Proportional symbol (bubble) world map**, shown as **three map panels** for different years.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses **small multiples / faceting by year**: panels for **1990**, **2023**, and **2050**.
- Each panel is a **world map** with circles placed geographically.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year (1990, 2023, 2050) | Temporal | **Faceting / panel title** |
| Geographic location (country position) | Categorical/nominal (geographic) | **Position on map** |
| Population magnitude (or country total represented by bubble size) | Quantitative | **Circle area/size** |
| Age structure / population age composition (younger → working age → older) | Ordinal | **Color/hue** of circles |
| Country name | Categorical/nominal | **Text label** |

### Visible legend information
- The color legend indicates an **ordered age-composition scale** from **younger populations** to **working age** to **older populations**.
raw_comment:
1) I notice that the graph shows the population of the world,  highlighting their ages. The size of the circles on the maps represents the size of the population and the color shows the age of the population, separated by groups. While analyzing the graphs, I noticed that the population increased over time. The 1990 graph shows smaller circles in each country therefore showing the smaller population. In both the 2023 and 2050 maps, the population seems to increase as the circles get much larger. I also noticed that most of the populations have working class or younger in the 1990 map. In the 2023 graph the younger population becomes of working age. In the 2050 predicted map, the population in China turned into the older generation as did the other countries except for India which continues to be of working age. Also the age group in Africa doesn't seem to change between the years and the predicted map.

2) Why does the age group in Africa not change like the rest of the continents do?  Why does the population continue to increase?

3) This is relevant because the population seems to increase over time and there seems to be more of working age instead of younger populations. This could mean that there might be less jobs and people might not want to have children.

4) "Gen Z Embracing the Aging Process"

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that everywhere in the world, the older populations are becoming more apparent and are seen to be populating up most of the land masses in our world. I noticed that over populations seems to be becoming a more apparent issue the longer we wait, we may be able to control it as of now, but with the predictions for the next 30 years being what is being shown, we need to handle the issue before it get out of hand. I see that specifically in the continent of Africa, Europe, and Asia, aging seems to be taking over, and by 2050, most of our world will be dominated by the older ages and generations. 

2. I wonder how in the continent of Africa, it seemed to stay controlled by the younger population and even grew more so I wonder if they may have an issue with all the newborns coming into their world and how overpopulation will affect them in the coming years.

3. When it comes to my community, we need balance. In a community where the young outweigh the old by a lot, we will not be able to pass down all the reliable and lesson worth teachings that would be apparent if an older population was present. However, if my community was dominated by an older generation with little to no young people, a lot of labor heavy work or things needed to be completed around our community will be left undone. If there is no balance, the community's entire equilibrium is thrown off.

4. Older Population Looks To Take Control, Is Aging The New Young?

raw_comment:
1)  I have noticed graphs that show the size of circles increasing over time, indicating population growth. The data on the map covers the years from 1990 to 2023, with predictions for 2050. It shows that every country except Africa has had or will have a shift in the age population, transitioning from a younger population to a working-age population by 2050. Furthermore, the predictions for 2050 suggest that countries like China and Europe will transition from a working-age population to an older population. Meanwhile, Japan will continue to have a high proportion of elderly residents, as it has since 2023.
2) I'm curious about governments' strategies to meet countries' needs/new standards as they transition from working-age to older populations. Also, when will these plans be implemented, and will any proactive measures be taken in response to the anticipated changes in the population's age? 
3)This will impact my community and me as in the future, China's working-age population as of 2023 produces goods imported to countries like where I live, the U.S., but as China's transition to older population will cause a decrease in our Global economy, and inflation may rise.
4) The Unavoidable Reality: More Old People Than Young People in the Future

raw_comment:
This graph presents 3 age distribution maps, labeled by the years 1990, 2023, and 2050. I notice they are not only all graduated symbol maps, which are displaying the population size of each country, but that they are also showing the country's average age distribution. In each map every country's population get's increasingly larger, and most country's population gets older as well. Although African country's are an exception, as their average population's are staying young.
I wonder if populations getting older is related to the worldwide advances in sanitation, hygiene, nutrition, and medical discoveries. I also wonder why African country's populations are staying young, even though the population is growing as steadily as the aging populations. I think that this graph is displaying different country's vary in population growth as well as the average population age and the connection between the two. This relates to me and my community, because in 2050, I will be working age. The graph predicts that in 2050 the population will be older than working age, which suggests a high dependency ratio, and that younger and older populations will depend on my generation. That is not beneficial for young, working, or older populations, and will negatively effect our economy.  A headline that envelopes this graph is "Younger populations on a decline"

raw_comment:
Period 2 Sayles

The global population age distribution is predicted to change drastically within the next three decades, with signs already appearing. The population age distribution in 1990 was mostly young, with superpower countries being working age. By 2050, it is projected for more of a mix of old, young, and working population ages with the old concentrated in the West, South America, and particularly East Asia (China making up a large portion of that). In contrast, Africa's high birth rate is projected to continue to create young populations across the continent, with increasingly more countries showing up on the map. Southeast Asia and the Middle East are more steady in population age than other regions. These regions developed into a working population by 2023, and are projected to remain mostly the same.

I wonder why South America is more similar in age distribution to the West rather than the Middle East and Africa. Is it related to political/economic instability vs. the exploitation of natural resources?

This relates to me and the younger generation because we are not having children at the same rate as the older generations, because of a perceived lack of stability (economically and politically).

raw_comment:
I notice this graph has 3 separate maps indicating the ages of people in different continents and in different time periods. I know this because of the 3 labeled maps that reads, 1990, 2023, and 2050. Throughout time they have predicted that by 2050 there would be more older people.

I wonder how accurate this graph is and if their prediction of age distribution is correct for the year 2050. I wonder why more elders are surviving longer than before and why mainly in China. 

The drastic incline of age distribution is very important to not only my community, but the world all together. Being that more people are likely to survive longer, that can affect the economic growth.

Why are some countries predominantly older populations yet some of the others are composed primarily from younger populations?

4)Our World is Aging And So are We

raw_comment:
I notice that most of the working age population is clustered around India and China in all 3 graphs.

I wonder what is causing the age distribution around the world to change. Is it a result of migration or are certain areas of the world just more favorable to different age groups?

This relates to me and my community as communities need a balance of young and old. A community with a mostly young population will be unable to have teachings and other things old people pass down. Meanwhile a community with a mostly old population will have no young people to do the labors and other things needed that old people can't do.

"The Aging Phenomenon"

What do I notice?

The first thing I noticed about these graphs was that the dots got progressively larger and more orange. This means that the populations of countries in future years will be higher than the population's of those same countries in the past years. Additionally, I noticed that more dots appeared on the map. In the areas that were mostly empty in 1990 became nearly fully filled with dots in 1950. The continent that changed the most dramatically in the concentration of dots is Africa. It went from nearly fully empty to nearly fully filled.

What do I wonder?

I wonder why the population concentration increased so dramatically in Africa. What factors played into people going there or what factors allowed people to live longer to more greatly populate the continent. Additionally I wonder in the mortality rate for birth went down, resulting in more healthy babies being born. I wonder why the mortality rate for older people is also decreasing. Is it because more and better treatments for different diseases are being found? Is it because they have to work less hard because we are in an age of advancing technology which is taking over human careers.

raw_comment:
This graph is especially interesting to me - I've been fascinated with population dispersion for a little while, and seeing it in a graph with a comparison to the past and a prediction for the future is incredible. 

I notice that a majority of the population as of now is centralized in India and China, and both areas - "hotspots" if you will - are marked to be of working age.

Compared to 1990, the populations are largely changed; India's population reached an average of the working age, and both area's populations expanded dramatically. Now, compared to the predictions for the future, I'm amazed.

I interpret the predictive graph of 2050 as such: India's population expands impressively, and the general populous remains of working age. China experiences a decreased population, and the national average features older populations. There's a population boom in most areas of central and southern Africa, and most of Europe becomes older generations. North America and South America remain largely unchanged - aside from the aging of their population. 

I wonder, after writing this, how accurately the world will follow the prediction. In addition, I'm curious what might cause the world to deviate from the prediction. What sort of global tragedies, such as wars or more pandemics, might change the population or age distribution of the world? How might the United States struggle through this, and how might my small town be harmed or helped by it?

"A Growing World - What We Expect"

While we age, so does Europe.

Thanks to all the students who responded.   Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received: 

“The Graying Globe: A Demographic Tug-of-War” by Ella from Freedom Prep Academy. 
"From Baby Boom to Baby Bust: The US Birth Rate Decline May Pose Challenges in 2050" by Matt from Andover High School. 
“Age Distribution Around the World” by Grace from Philadelphia.
“The Imminent Earth: Past, Present, and Future Populations” by Nia from Curtis High School.
“The Globe is Aging, and We May Not Be Ready for It” by  Avani SL from Baldwin School PA.
“Be On the Lookout for Retirement Homes in 2050!” by Avani SL from Baldwin School PA.
“Are we aging faster than our world can handle?” by Tatum Ahearn from Andover High School.
“Is death catching up to us faster than we can predict?” by Tatum Ahearn from Andover High School.
“Older, Younger, Or Just Right? What Dominating Age Will Take Over Populations By 2050?” by Katherine H from Academy of Saint Elizabeth.
“Population Predictions and Problems” by Izzy Clark from AOSE Academy of Saint Elizabeth.
 
The next graph will be released by Friday, September 15.  Hope to read your responses next week when the topic will be Football and C.T.E..
 
Signing off – Erica Chauvet from Pittsburgh, who is cheering for more babies to boost the younger population, and Nick Simonetti of Greensboro, North Carolina, who enjoys graphs with color bubbles even though he is red-green color blind.

This affects my community because in the US the population switches from in 1990 from a working age to in 2050 being in between working age and older population. raw_comment:
This graph models the age and size of populations in the world. I notice in more developed countries, the population is generally getting older, while in less developed areas, like  Africa, the population is getting younger. I also noticed that as time goes on, the circles indicating population also get bigger in Africa but either stay generally the same or see a small growth in other places. 

I wonder if the larger amount of young population in Africa is due to lower life spans caused by a lack of medicine and resources like birth control. In contrast, I wonder if the increasing majority older population in China is due to the one-child policy, which caused the younger generation to shrink significantly. The reason the population shifted older in most of the rest of the world might also be due to people giving birth to fewer children, less often. 

 As the population shifts older in countries like China and America, the number of working-age people is dwindling in comparison to those in retirement. Soon national economies could crash because there are not enough people working to support them. The U.S. population aged 65 and over grew nearly five times faster than the total population from 1920 to 2020 (2020 Census).  This would affect my community because it would cause work shortages and lead to a growing demand for consumer goods, resulting in fewer exports, which would be even more detrimental to the economy. 

Fun Title: Live a Longer Life: An Economical Disaster

raw_comment:
Population Goes Up, World Goes Down

Our group noticed that the graph shows the average age group that dominates the country and the bigger the bubble/circle, the bigger the population. There are 3 graphs, one shows 1990, the one next to it shows this year, 2023, and the last graph shows 2050. As time moves forward, more bubbles pop up and the already existing bubbles tend to get bigger. 

As a group we came up with a couple questions regarding the different graphs. We wonder why the population is always growing, and why there are still largely older people in certain countries. We also wonder what could cause the average age to differ through the years and what effects it could have on those countries. Lastly we wonder if in 2050 there will be enough space for the growth of population they are predicting. 

We believe that there probably will be more harmful effects to the growing population than positive effects, one of those being that it could create a more negative effect on the environment because of the higher amount of people as time goes on. There would definitely be more pollution and climate change could quickly rise. Another effect it could have on the future is that it could create an impact on the economy, especially if there are less working age individuals.

Nick T, Sophia H, Stella C

## 1) Chart type
- **Proportional symbol (bubble) world map**, shown as **three map panels** for different years.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses **small multiples / faceting by year**: panels for **1990**, **2023**, and **2050**.
- Each panel is a **world map** with circles placed geographically.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year (1990, 2023, 2050) | Temporal | **Faceting / panel title** |
| Geographic location (country position) | Categorical/nominal (geographic) | **Position on map** |
| Population magnitude (or country total represented by bubble size) | Quantitative | **Circle area/size** |
| Age structure / population age composition (younger → working age → older) | Ordinal | **Color/hue** of circles |
| Country name | Categorical/nominal | **Text label** |

### Visible legend information
- The color legend indicates an **ordered age-composition scale** from **younger populations** to **working age** to **older populations**.
raw_comment:
1. What I notice is how age distribution is very similar in the countries on the same continent in 1990. South America is mostly younger, Europe is mostly working, and so on. 2023 is similar as well even if the age has increased. Additionally, I see how the older population has gotten more prevalent throughout the world as time has gone on and could keep going all the way to 2050. For example, the US could change from turquoise to green by 2050, so who knows by 2070 where it could go. 
2. What I wonder is if they were trying to target a specific country or continent and show the drastic change. There is a large portion of working age in China right now and it could vastly change to older populations and I wonder how that could effect the world in years to come. I also wonder why Africa was the main area that could possibly not change very much over the course of 60 years and most other continents completely changed. 
3. What I think is going on in this graph is the shift of population growth throughout the different countries and because of increased birth rates and migration the economic growth can be effected. More people means that more people are going to be needed to fill jobs and other services. 
4. This relates to my community because the area I live in has a very large population and there are many apartments and such, so I am curious how that could change over maybe 10 to 20 years. 

Catchy Phrase: Growing, Growing, and MORE Growing

raw_comment:
I notice that the older population of Europe, China, and the US, is projected to increase between 2023 and 2050. The circle clusters also increase, suggesting a population increase. Africa appears to have the greatest increase in population, interestingly maintaining a "younger population" across all three years.

I wonder why the older population is increasing in Europe and the US in particular. I realize that the Baby Boom generation created a comparative increase in the now "working age/older population," which would likely explain the data. China is still evidently being affected by the One Child Policy, as people had fewer children so the older population is projected to increase. I wonder if the increase in an older population will affect countries' economy.

The graph depicts the aging demographics of the world. Countries with large economies, such as the US, Europe and China, experience the most dramatic increase in older populations in 2050.

This relates to my community because I, and everyone else considered a young adult, will later have to take care of the large population of senior citizens in the states. There will have to be government reforms in relation to retirement so that no one is left behind.

Headline: "Time Are A-Changin': Young Folks Move Aside!"

raw_comment:
These graphs display the age distribution of the world's population and how it has evolved and will continue to evolve. The size of these dots represents the size of the population in that region. I noticed that the population in the U.S. in 1990 was predominantly those of the working age. Currently, in 2023, the majority of the U.S. population is between the younger population age bracket and the working age bracket. I infer this means most of our population is in their mid to late twenties. It is predicted that in 2050 the U.S. population will be predominantly the age bracket between working age and older populations. I infer this means that the majority of our population will be in their 40s. This is not a typical age where people retire so it should not pose a large threat to the economy. I infer or population will become older because fewer and fewer people are having children. Some people are participating in a Birth Strike in hopes of improving global warming. I notice that overall populations are increasing over time. I wonder if this will change as global warming gets worse, and potentially more people will opt to not have children. I notice that China's population is predicted to be predominantly older in 2050. I wonder if this is because of the One Child Policy, as this ended not too long ago in 2016. 
Population Predictions and Problems

In the graph, I noticed that the age distribution in the world’s population remains unchanged for Africa and in some parts of Asia up until 2050. I also saw that in most cases, countries that had a higher youth population in 1990, often led into a higher older population in 2050. This trend is demonstrated in China, the U.S., and parts of Europe. I wonder how the age distribution information was obtained and how the future graph (based in 2050) was predicted. What type of research went on behind this? Also, I wonder if the baby boom in the mid-to-late 1900s in the U.S. and Europe contributed to their trends… along with the lower birth rates with the decrease of fertility rates in the world. Lastly, a headline that best captures the graph’s main idea is, “The Rise of the Middle-Aged Population in Developed Countries in the Coming Decades”

## 1) Chart type
- **Proportional symbol (bubble) world map**, shown as **three map panels** for different years.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses **small multiples / faceting by year**: panels for **1990**, **2023**, and **2050**.
- Each panel is a **world map** with circles placed geographically.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year (1990, 2023, 2050) | Temporal | **Faceting / panel title** |
| Geographic location (country position) | Categorical/nominal (geographic) | **Position on map** |
| Population magnitude (or country total represented by bubble size) | Quantitative | **Circle area/size** |
| Age structure / population age composition (younger → working age → older) | Ordinal | **Color/hue** of circles |
| Country name | Categorical/nominal | **Text label** |

### Visible legend information
- The color legend indicates an **ordered age-composition scale** from **younger populations** to **working age** to **older populations**.
raw_comment: In this graph, there are three different maps of the world representing the population ages during 1990, 2023, and 2050. In the map of 1990, the majority of the population across the world were younger ages because all of the dots are dark blue and teal colored on all the countries, representing younger populations and working populations. In 2023, some of the countries’ population ages remained the same such as in Nigeria and China, but a lot of the countries’ populations shifted towards older ages such as in India, Japan, and France because the colors of the dots turned lighter, signifying a shift towards older populations. Finally, the predicted populations in 2050 demonstrate a much older population across the world, particularly in China and France because their dots are fully yellow. I noticed that the general trend in population is that as years pass, the population of elderly people increases. I wonder what the cause of this is and predict that it might be because there are more advancements in medicine and technology that allow elderly people to live longer. I also wonder why some countries’ populations advance to older populations while others stay in the younger or working age populations and if less working age populations will leave an absence of employees in jobs across the globe. My headline for this graph would be: “Older Populations Taking Over the World?”

raw_comment:
I noticed that in 1990, South America, Central America, Africa, Europe, and Asia all had younger populations. In 2023, the younger population grew into the working age population. In 2050, the population will have a new younger generation and the working age will become seniors. In Africa, their population stays really similar from the 90’s to 2050 as the younger population is more evident.

2. What do you wonder?
I wonder why Africa experiences significantly greater growth than other continents? I also wonder what the life expectancy is for each continent? Do people in China not reproduce enough to make a second generation?

3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
This impacts me and my community because I am the average age population for the U.S in 2023. According to the prediction, my generation won't have given birth to enough children to make up the majority by the year 2050, which leads me to believe that American women are having children later than women in other developed nations.

This graph is showing the different age populations in 1990, 2023 and the predictions for 2050 in different countries. 

“Population Age Distributions Around the World: No More youth?”

raw_comment: The graph depicts the mass of the younger generations, and how the population's average age will follow that generation's average age. As shown on the graph, a large portion of the population is working age now, so their numbers will continue to dominate as they age. Another contributor to their domination of world populations is the rapidly decreasing family size, spearheaded by the current young adults. It is no longer desirable or feasible to have more than a couple of children, so the generations to follow will be considerably smaller. I wonder how this will affect the economy because it will become reliant on an excess of workers, so when the population of workers begins to decline, the workforce will be left wanting. I can see the generation size differences in my own life and in my family. Where my grandparents had multiple siblings, I only have one. The high school in my town is overpopulated, yet there is an excess number of preschools. The change in populations and the growth of the current young adults will lead the world into a new culture of dominant elderly voices, and a small youth to answer back. A possible headline for this graph would be, “By the year 2050, the old will be hollering, but the youth will only be able to whisper back.”

raw_comment:
Population Age

I believe that if the country has a population that is mostly of working age, then the economy will be prosperous. Because the country will have more people making money and paying taxes, inflation will be lower. If the country has a younger population, then there will be fewer people making money and fewer taxes being paid, which will cause the economy to start to struggle a little bit and inflation in taxes for the government to keep making enough money, which will cause companies to increase prices to be able to make a profit. I also think the economy will prosper if the population is mostly older because retirement plans are considered income, which will be taxed, preventing an increase in taxes and overall prices.

raw_comment:
This illustrates the average age range of countries, or regions, all over the globe. The graph's most interesting is how many countries fall into the younger population (15 and under). While countries such as India and France are seen to be changing in average age range, that is the majority of their society increasing in age, countries in Africa and the Middle East, such as Nigeria, continuously stay in younger population range. With a younger population constantly being the majority, what is more prevalent, is short life spans or mothers constantly giving birth? As for China,  the older age range (65 and above) will dominate by 2050. This is a direct result of their 1 child rule in families. This multi-children ban was an attempt to combat the issue of overpopulation. However, it was proven to not only be worrisome in communities, as people were killing and or abandoning their kids, but leading directly to the problem depicted on the graph. With an older population taking over, how will this affect the economy? Who will take over the jobs that 65-year-olds are unable to do? If this starts affecting China in a negative way, when will it start to affect the world as a whole? As for my own community, the only issue I feel that will affect it is the issue of China. The graph shows that even though the US population is getting older, the national age average seems to dip back and forth.

“Older, Younger, Or Just Right? What Dominating Age Will Take Over Populations By 2050?”

raw_comment:
I have noticed that over time the aging population is increasing. The chart shows that the 1990 map has no older population points, but the 2023 map has older population points, and the 2050 map has a lot of older population points. This is probably due to medical advances that are helping people live longer.  
 I wonder if we will reach the point where the older population outnumbers the younger. In theory, it should stay the same because people are born and die every day, so it should stay relatively constant. That's why I wonder if the future will be the same as now or completely different.  
 In a few years, my generation will be part of the working generation, and new people will join this "young generation". 
 
 This graph shows the evolution of the eras in different parts of the world in different years. The title I would use for this is "The Future of Overcrowding"

raw_comment:
1. I notice that in 1990, the US, Europe, and China all had working aged populations while places like
India, Africa, and South America had largely younger population. By 2050, Europe and China will have
largely older populations, with the US trailing towards that direction. In 2050, only Africa really has a
sizeable younger population.
2. Why does Africa show no change while other parts of the world do. How will this affect the economy,
particularly in the United States? WIll an older population contribute to economic stagnation?
3. This relates to me because I will be 45 by 2050, so the effects of an older population could have
consequences towards the country during that time.
4. Earth 2050: Rise of the Old People

2050 Will Have The Most Variety In Age Population

raw_comment:
1 ) What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?
I notice that China is predicted to be mostly older populations in 2050 which is seen by the large yellow circle that is labeled with the country. I notice that the working age and younger take up most of the population in all three graphs which can be seen by the blue and green circles taking up most of the graph. I notice that in Africa the younger population is a majority of the countries total population. This can be seen by the blue circles littered throughout the continent. 

2 ) What do you wonder?
I wonder why the working age takes up a majority of the population even though the world's population is rapidly increasing. Doesn't that mean that the younger generation should be the largest? I wonder if China's child limitation rule is one of the main reasons for the prediction that the majority of the population will be old in 2050.

3 ) How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to our community because as an American, when I am in my working age, the majority of the population will most likely be older than me. This can be because less people are having kids in our current time. 

4) What’s going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.

Population Age A-Round The World

Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?” 

Today’s graphs are maps which show the shift in population age distribution worldwide. What regions are gaining in working-age population and therefore, could experience greater economic growth?

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online for the four questions. We have added a suggestion to the “What do you notice?” question. If your notice includes a claim, please back it up with evidence that supports your claim.

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the free link to the online article that included these maps.

You can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box
below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”

raw_comment:
Click on the attached link and answer these 4 questions: 

1. What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?

I noticed that in 1990, the US and Brazil were among high density countries, but were not as noticeably dense as China and India. In 2023, The US grew in population, and the US population has grown older. In 2050, the US population will remain roughly the same, and they will become primarily older aged.

2. What do you wonder?

I wonder why Japan is the only one to be indicated as yellow, meaning they have the oldest population in the world. I also wonder why Africa and Europe will grow so much in population while the US or Brazil remain roughly the same.

3. What impact does this have on you and your community?

This graph indicates that the US' population will remain roughly the same --- and with older aged people --- in 27 years. I wonder if this is because of the declining birth rates in the US now, and if western media has an impact on that. If our goal is to grow a bigger population, or to create younger generations in order to ensure a brighter future, then this could be a problem that needs to be addressed. Otherwise, the impact this has is not significant.

4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.

"From Baby Boom to Baby Bust: The US Birth Rate Decline May Pose Challenges in 2050"

raw_comment: I noticed that in 1990 they had more of a younger population than in 2023. China seems to be the country with the largest working-age population during 1990. In 2023, they have less of a younger population and more of an older population. This time though, India and China are the countries with the most working-age populations. Now in 2050, it is obvious that there are more colors referring to the younger populations, working age, and older populations. These categories seem to be more spread out than in 1990 and 2023. China seems to have changed into a country with the most older population and India seems to be the same. The U.S. seems to be in the middle of working age and older populations just like Brazil. I wonder what China and Japan have done to be able to support older people. I also wonder if India has a more working-age population than China since they had a one-child policy and India had the chance to catch up. This relates to me and my community because through 1990 and 2050 there has been a high population between young people and working age due to the higher chance to succeed. There are more job opportunities in the U.S. therefore, many migrate to the U.S. for the opportunities and start a family here so their children can get the opportunities offered as well. These opportunities include education and jobs. Heading: The Differences of the Evolution of a Population

raw_comment:
What did I notice?
There is a projected trend of an aging population in China, Canada and Europe. However, the distribution of the populations of India, Indonesia, Pakistan are expected to shift from a younger population to a working age population. While the population will likely increase in Africa, much of the growth is anticipated to be a younger population.
What do I wonder?
I am curious as to how the data was collected, and how accurate it is. What ages are correlated with the “younger populations” or “working populations”? Furthermore, I wonder how current data was used to create the trends for 2050.
How does this affect my country?
In my country, those who are not part of the working population are viewed negatively by society because they don’t aid the economy. As the population ages, instead of the expectation that the older population would willingly spend money and stimulate the economy, many are saving their money, shifting the economy as fewer are available to work.
Can I come up with a catchy title?
“The Age of Aging”

raw_comment:
1. The average age of countries' populations is getting older and projected to get even older by 2050. Right now, the majority of the population is of working age, but in 2050 there will be fewer people able to work and build the economy. The population of Africa is projected to grow a lot in comparison to other countries. The US population is overall younger today than it was in 1990, which is against the trend of the other countries.

2. I wonder if a lot more of the world's workforce will come from younger countries in the future, such as India, Pakistan, and Indonesia. Today, all of our products are made in China, but maybe that will change. I also wonder if the economic strength of big global powers will diminish with an older population. 

3. In 25 years, people my age will become the workforce and build towards positions of power in the country. We can definitely make a lot of changes in the US, and it is up to us (and not the older people) to 1) strengthen the country, and 2) make it a more equitable place to live.

4.

The Globe is Aging, and We May Not Be Ready for It.

Be On the Lookout for Retirement Homes in 2050!

raw_comment:
1) What do you notice?
In the map, I noticed around the world, through time, the age distribution around the world is changing, and increasing. For example, China from 1990 to 2023, kept its average working age to increase through that interval of time. As well as with India, in 1990, it started with a young population, but after 33 years, it started to increase to fit in the working age.  Also, by looking at the graph, we see that the prediction in 2050, each continent, except Africa, is expected to experience a significant rise in population age according to this graph. 
2) What do you wonder?
I wonder why throughout time; Africa had the largest increase in population throughout the period of 1990 to 2023. Are there any factors that cause their population to increase more than any other country?
3) How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community in a way that through time, as the population grows, the production of resources that are traded around the world would increase as we have more people to both work in the production, but as well as we have more consumers. And maybe at some point, as jobs are available, competition does too, maybe some people would lose their jobs in my community to have younger people keep up with it. 
4) What’s going on in this graph?
The Remarkable Surge of World Population Across Continents!

raw_comment:
These graphs are maps of the population of the world and their ages. The size of the dots represents the size of the population in that area. The color of the dots relates to the key that signifies which color represents which age group. The map from 1990 shows a smaller population in each country compared to the maps of 2023 and 2050. All of the populations in each country have the majority as working age or younger. However, in the map of 2023, the majority of each country’s population gets older. The majority of the population in France begins to approach the older population and China’s majority reaches the older population. In addition, the overall population of the world is increasing. In the 2050 map, most of the world's population is the working age or older. However, in Africa, the population is still mostly young population. The population of the planet as a whole also increases a lot. I can conclude from this that the African population stays young because they are a third-world country. Therefore, their technology isn’t as good and their health deteriorates quickly as they get older. This means more deaths. On the other hand, the older population in China is a result of the one-child rule. This is going to prove difficult for the new generation to take care of the large older population. 

“Population Plague"

1. What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?

I notice that the more expensive places to live generally house the older population or working population. For example, most products that are sold throughout the US are designed and manufactured in China, hence most of the working class takes up the Chinese population. It is also very expensive to live throughout Asia because in most areas they are trying to eliminate carbon waste by stopping people from using a car as their method of transportation (Singapore). 

2. What do you wonder?

I wonder why most of the graph is taken up by the younger community in the 90s, but they have predicted that in 2050 there will be a dramatic difference. I also wonder how they differentiate the working class from the younger community since I know that most people my age are considered to be really young but most of us have jobs.

We may have to reconsider opening up more government housing and figuring out a solution globally. The fact that in the 2023 most of the US is in the younger/working class, and in just 20ish years we are predicted to be apart of the older generation, is slightly concerning. 

4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.

Are we aging faster than our world can handle? 

Is death catching up to us faster than we can predict?

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?

The first thing I’ve noticed is that the graph displays how our population on earth has grown tremendously by putting it into a new perspective with the bubbles and seeing how they fill up more space on the map. 
I noticed that China has a very large elderly population while Nigeria, Ethiopia and D.R.C have lots of young people.

2. What do you wonder?

I wonder if there will ever be some type of “population control” in society. Whether that’s a limit to how many children a family can have or a max population for a town.

3. What impact does this have on you and your community?

The impact this has on me and my community is inflation. Materials and resources needed to produce common objects or food to the public have grown more scarce due to the higher demand since there’s so many people, the prices say everything.

4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.

Where We’ll Be In 2050

raw_comment:
I noticed a significant shift in global age distribution. Developed nations, such as the U.S., Europe, and East Asia, have increasingly aging populations from 1990 to 2050, as indicated by the colors transitioning from green to orange on the graph. In contrast, regions like Africa and parts of Latin America maintain predominantly younger populations, reflected in the consistent blue coloring. This transformation might be attributed to the ongoing development and modernization of these countries.

I wonder what is causing the population to get older? Is it due to declining birth rates? Increased life expectancy? Lower immigration? Urbanization?

This affects my community as an aging population can strain healthcare, affect the labor force, and stress pension systems in your community. It may require adjustments in housing, social services, and urban planning. Encouraging intergenerational interactions and seizing economic opportunities are crucial for a well-balanced and thriving community.

Catchy headlines: From Cradle to Canes: The Global Agequake Chronicles

The Silver Storm: Unmasking the Ageing Phenomenon

Youth Fades, Wisdom Stays: A World in Transition

Chronicles of Aging Nations: The Quiet Revolution

From Baby Boom to Silver Surge: Global Agequake Ahead

The Graying Globe: A Demographic Tug-of-War

raw_comment:
1) I noticed that the age distribution around the world is changing. While developed countries are becoming much older, less developed countries continue to have a high proportion of younger populations. In the graph, it shows that throughout 1990-2050, the U.S., Europe, and  East Asia had older populations (colors ranged from green to orange) while Africa and some parts of Latin America had younger populations (color was predominantly blue).
2) I wonder what the correlation is between economic growth and the world's age distribution. Does greater economic growth mean lower birth rates? Wouldn't it make more sense for developed countries to have more kids since they have the financial ability to take care of them? Or does having an aging population much more detrimental than it seems?
3) This relates to me and my community because we live in the U.S., a developed nation with a rapidly growing old population. Already there are many problems with the large population of old people. The most prominent problem is a decline in the working age population. Less people working leads to shortages of workers. If the trend continues, this might severely impact the economy.
4) Age Is Just A Number, Or Is There More To It?

- **Proportional symbol (bubble) world map**, shown as **three map panels** for different years.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses **small multiples / faceting by year**: panels for **1990**, **2023**, and **2050**.
- Each panel is a **world map** with circles placed geographically.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year (1990, 2023, 2050) | Temporal | **Faceting / panel title** |
| Geographic location (country position) | Categorical/nominal (geographic) | **Position on map** |
| Population magnitude (or country total represented by bubble size) | Quantitative | **Circle area/size** |
| Age structure / population age composition (younger → working age → older) | Ordinal | **Color/hue** of circles |
| Country name | Categorical/nominal | **Text label** |

### Visible legend information
- The color legend indicates an **ordered age-composition scale** from **younger populations** to **working age** to **older populations**.

1. What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?
This graph demonstrates the change in human population over time all over the world from 1990 to an estimation of 2050. It measures both the age range and number of people to highlight different groups of people that makeup the population. It shows that by 2050 there will be a very large population growth in all places around the world. 
2. What do you wonder?
I wonder why we are going to have more people in 2050 than other years. I also wonder if this large population will help or hurt the world. Ex: not enough food/space for more people 
3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
 This can impact my community because the food distribution and the resources would be lessened with the higher populations. With more people there is more stress on resources which over time can negatively affect people/future generations.
4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.
Predicting Populations... How Will This end?

raw_comment:
What do I notice? In the Americas the populations seems to mature quite significantly yet the overall size remains relatively the same. And with Eurasia, the current aging crisis seems to have significantly worsen over the years, especially in Northern Europe and west Asia. The Middle East and east Asia maintain a relatively young population whilst also growing in size. Lastly the African population seems to not only have grown tremendously but it bears the most youthful population out of all the continents.

What do I wonder? I'm curious as to why more developed nations display a trend of having a much more elderly population as opposed to less developed ones. And why other continents display relatively stable growth and Africa much more significant growth.

How does this relate to you and your community? Looking at South Africa, there does not seem to be any change of note so with regards to my immediate community it's hard to say, however looking at at all corners of the continent except the south , it would be possible for more people to have migrated to Africa due to the cheaper cost of living. And this assumption would make sense as a more elderly population would likely have more or earn more money than their youthful counterparts and thus could sustain their livelihood in Europe and Asia.

Catchy headline? Africa: The financial safehaven of tomorrow.
